SETU: Learning Telugu by Correcting a Rule-Governed AI Classmate
Models write, rules decide: what held up, and what did not
IIIT Hyderabad
Language Models and Agents · Monsoon 2026
ABSTRACT

SETU teaches Telugu to Hindi speakers. At the sentence stage the learner corrects Raju, an AI classmate who makes a Hindi speaker's mistakes. Raju's knowledge is data in a database, kept one step behind the learner's.

One rule governs the design: a language model may write text, but ordinary code decides what is shown, how an answer is marked and what the learner's record says.

We built the tutor, attacked it, compared five model capabilities with simpler baselines, and checked the marker against a native speaker. No learner has used it yet: learning outcomes are simulated only.

METHODOLOGY

• Ladder: letters → syllables → words → phrases → sentence rules (Raju) → scenes.

• Raju's sentence, the coach's hint and the friend's line are model proposals. Each passes a filter or is replaced by teacher-approved text.

• A rule-based checker marks every answer: correct, partial, wrong or unsure. Unsure goes to a teacher.

• One writer, under a restricted database role, updates the record. Models have no write tools.

• Evaluation: one hosted model (gemini-3.5-flash), frozen sets of 29–58 cases, Wilson intervals, exact McNemar tests, 50 native-speaker labels, two learner simulators.

The running app: Raju's sentence, the coach's hint, the learner's home page.

RESULTS

Control held. 17/17 tool attacks refused; 11 injected instructions, no unsafe attempt. No model text reached a learner unchecked.

The model did not need to choose. A fixed loop that shows the model its own rejected draft: 0.92 valid. Model-chosen tool calls: 0.94, at 4.7× the tokens.

Most capabilities did not beat baselines. Stepwise reasoning 0.36 vs 0.40 direct. Retrieval hints 12/29 vs 10/29. Fine-tuning: stopped, too little validated data.

The checker is safe but coarse. It never accepted a wrong answer, yet agrees poorly with a native speaker: κ = 0.15 (target 0.6).

Purple: language model, text only. Teal: deterministic code. Dashed line: the only code that can change learner state.

MODEL CAPABILITIES

• Prompt only: 0.71. Old app loop (no memory): 0.78.

• Add memory of the rejected draft (the app now): 0.92 at 223 tokens.

• Model-chosen tools: 0.94 at 1044 tokens.

• "Valid" means equal to the bank's sentence: the model adds no new sentence.

CHECKER · SIMULATION

• Checker κ 0.15 vs model judge 0.46; one labeller, 50 answers.

• It rejects half the answers the native speaker accepted.

• Simulation only: correcting Raju (A) ranks last, 0.25 vs 0.33 and 0.31, in 28/28 assumption settings. An older simulator disagrees.

CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

• A model can be confined to proposing text, with marks and records owned by code.

• For Raju's sentence, memory of the last draft mattered; model-chosen tool calls did not add to it.

• Not shown: that correcting a classmate helps anyone learn. No learner data exists.

• Done after the audit: the app now uses the memory loop; the filter is unchanged. Next: independent native review and a second labeller; widen accepted answers; then a small pilot with consent and clearance.
